destination.title: She Was Handcuffed and Jailed Over a $50 Seatbelt Fine

short49: A mom drives her two kids down
a Texas road nobody buckled up.
That's the whole crime.
The worst the law allows is a fifty-dollar fine.
So can police cuff you and jail
you over that?
An officer pulls her over.
He doesn't reach for a ticket book.
He reaches for handcuffs.
He cuffs her in front of her
kids drives her to the station takes
her booking photo and locks her in a cell.
Her penalty for the seatbelt? Fifty dollars.
So she sued.
A full arrest for a fine-only offense
she argued is unreasonable.
Everyone agreed he had probable cause.
But is that alone enough to put
you in a cell?
In two thousand one the Supreme Court
sided with the city five to four.
Even a pointless humiliating arrest over fifty
dollars is constitutional.
The police can do this.
Justice O'Connor dissented.
The fix the Court said is up to lawmakers.
Watch the full case on the channel.
Follow for more.

candidate_payload_lines: You assume no one gets handcuffed and booked into a cell over a seatbelt.
And in the year 2001, by a single vote, it told you that you were wrong.
In 1997, Gail Atwater was driving her pickup through Lago Vista with her two young children in the front seat.
No matter what any court later decided, Gail Atwater was never going to serve a single hour of jail as her sentence.
The handcuffs, the squad car, the cell, the booking photo, none of that was her punishment.
You know the Fourth Amendment even if you have never read it.
The case reached the Supreme Court, and in April of 2001 the Court gave its answer.
But probable cause, she argued, was never meant to be the end of the question.
After the spring of 2001, the answer from the highest court in the country is yes.
Holding stated as UPHELD / constitutional / "the police could do this" (never illegal or unconstitutional).

shorts.angle: Every heavy thing done to Gail Atwater that afternoon happened before any finding of guilt, because the only sentence the law could ever impose on her was money.
shorts.funnel_question_left_for_longform: If a cell was never available as her punishment, what did the Supreme Court say the police were still permitted to do to her?
shorts.loop_join: L8 says her real sentence arrived later and was money, which returns to L1's opening fact that the law could never have jailed her for a seatbelt.

lines.text: The law could never send Gail Atwater to jail for a seatbelt. Everything that happened to her happened before anyone decided she was guilty.
source_lines: No matter what any court later decided, Gail Atwater was never going to serve a single hour of jail as her sentence.
It happened before anyone had decided she was guilty of anything at all.

lines.text: Texas made riding unbelted a misdemeanor. The punishment the law set was a fine, no more than fifty dollars.
source_lines: Texas law made driving unbelted, and letting your children ride unbelted, a misdemeanor.
And the punishment the law set for it was a fine.
No less than twenty five dollars, no more than fifty.

lines.text: This was not the officer's first stop of her. He had pulled her over about a seatbelt before, and that time he was wrong.
source_lines: This was not their first meeting. Turek had stopped Atwater once before over a seatbelt, and that time he had been wrong.

lines.text: She asked to take her frightened children to a friend's house nearby first. He told her she was not going anywhere.
source_lines: She asked to take her frightened kids to a friend's house nearby first. He told her she was not going anywhere.

lines.text: A neighbor came out and took the two small children inside, so they would not have to watch the rest.
source_lines: A neighbor came out and took the two children inside, so they would not have to watch the rest.

lines.text: At the station she gave up her shoes, emptied her pockets, sat for a photograph, and spent about an hour alone in a cell.
source_lines: There she was made to take off her shoes, empty her pockets, and hand over everything she was carrying.
They put her in a holding cell, alone, and left her there for about an hour.

lines.text: Later she pleaded no contest and paid the fine. Fifty dollars. That was the entire penalty the law ever attached to what she did.
source_lines: She later pleaded no contest to the seatbelt offense and paid the fine. Fifty dollars.
That was the entire penalty the law had ever attached to what she did.

lines.text: The handcuffs, the squad car, the cell and the photograph were not her sentence. Her sentence arrived later, and it was money.
source_lines: The handcuffs, the squad car, the cell, the booking photo, none of that was her punishment.

shorts.angle: The majority handed the remedy to legislatures, so protection against an arrest like hers is now a matter of which state's statute book a driver happens to be inside.
shorts.funnel_question_left_for_longform: What did the majority itself call the arrest, in the same opinion in which it held that the Constitution permits it?
shorts.loop_join: L8 places the surviving rule on one side of a state border, which is the geography L1 opens with when it says the answer depends on the statute book rather than the Fourth Amendment.

lines.text: Whether a driver can be handcuffed over a fifty dollar offense now depends on the state's statute book, not on the Fourth Amendment.
source_lines: Which means the protection you might have assumed was written into the Fourth Amendment is, across much of the country, only as strong as whatever your state has put into a statute.

lines.text: The majority chose a rule that is easy to apply at the roadside: arrest is allowed wherever there is probable cause.
source_lines: A clear rule, arrest allowed wherever there is probable cause, is easier to apply and harder to abuse than a rule that asks every officer to weigh the penalty first.

lines.text: Anything else, it reasoned, would force officers to guess in a split second whether an offense carried jail or only a fine.
source_lines: A rule that let arrests turn on how serious the offense was would force officers to make fine legal judgments in a split second at the roadside, guessing whether a given crime carried jail or only a fine, and getting sued if they guessed wrong.

lines.text: The dissent called that a trade. The Court, O'Connor wrote, neglects the Fourth Amendment's express command in the name of administrative ease.
source_lines: Speaking for the dissent, she wrote that the Court neglects the Fourth Amendment's express command in the name of administrative ease.

lines.text: In doing so, she added, it cloaks the pointless indignity that Gail Atwater suffered with the mantle of reasonableness.
source_lines: In so doing, it cloaks the pointless indignity that Gail Atwater suffered with the mantle of reasonableness.

lines.text: The majority's answer was that legislatures can forbid these arrests, and many states have. The Constitution simply does not.
source_lines: Legislatures can forbid these arrests, and many states have. The Constitution simply does not.

lines.text: Some states now tell officers to write the ticket and let minor offenders drive away. Where those laws exist, they are the protection.
source_lines: Some states have passed laws telling their officers to write the ticket and let minor offenders drive away.
Where those laws exist, you are covered by them, not by the Constitution.

lines.text: Where no such law was written, the rule from that decision still stands, and the line it draws now runs along a state border.
source_lines: Where they do not, the rule of Atwater still stands.
What she left behind is a line the Supreme Court drew and has not erased.
